title: All the gear. No inner tube.
excerpt: The expedition luggage contains a coffee maker. The puncture repair equipment is somebody else’s problem.
body:
Anyone near the TET with a front inner tube, tyre levers, a pump and experience fitting them? Ideally someone who can come to me.

First proper off-road trip on the big bike. Front’s gone flat despite being in Enduro mode, which I’ll be raising with the dealer.

Before the usual comments, I have prepared. Full aluminium luggage, expedition screen, auxiliary lights and the premium navigation subscription. Didn’t bring tools because we were trying to travel light.

Location is difficult to explain. I’m on the green bit of the map. Can send a screenshot once someone tells me how to get the route back up.

Please no lectures about training. I’ve been driving for 23 years and watched most of a video about standing up.

There are two of us, but we agreed beforehand that neither would lift anything heavy because we’re on holiday.

EDIT: Sorted for coffee. Just need the tube, tools, pump and person.

EDIT 2: Someone on a small Honda stopped but immediately started talking about tyre pressures, so we’re waiting for an adventure rider.

title: Is anyone else finding Enduro Pro a bit disappointing?
excerpt: Six riding modes, no training, and a hole that keeps getting bigger.
body:
Is anyone else finding Enduro Pro a bit disappointing?

Selected it before this section and the bike has just dug a hole. Tried more throttle in case the system needed something to work with. Hole is now bigger.

Tyres are what the dealer recommended for my actual riding, which until this morning was mainly the A3.

Yes, I can see the gravel on the left. I went into the rut because there were tyre marks in it, which I took as a recommendation.

Can someone local come and help lift the back end out? Ideally three of you. Need to be moving fairly soon as the hotel stops serving lunch at two.

Please stop suggesting I take the panniers off. They were fitted by the dealer and I don’t want to affect the warranty.

Also, is there someone who maintains these lanes? For a European touring route the surface is very inconsistent.

EDIT: Training course is £300. Just struggling to justify that when the bike already has six riding modes.

title: The GPX line went straight across.
excerpt: A ford, a fully loaded bike and a rider who bought a motorcycle specifically to avoid walking.
body:
Anyone near this ford with a tow rope? Bike’s fine, I’ve just decided not to continue from its current position.

Went in because the GPX line went straight across. Surely whoever uploads these checks the water?

Got halfway, felt the front move and stopped to reassess. Unfortunately my reassessment foot didn’t reach the bottom where expected.

Managed to get it on the stand and walk out. Boots are full, which is disappointing given what they cost.

Before everyone says “you should have walked it first”, I specifically bought a motorbike to avoid walking these routes.

Also saw a video of someone crossing here last August and it barely came up the tyres. Same crossing, same bike, so I don’t see what I was supposed to do differently.

Could do with two people to help push. Please bring your own waterproofs. Mine are currently drying on the footbridge.

EDIT: Yes, I saw the bridge. It’s for pedestrians. I do respect access rules.

EDIT 2: Whoever commented “try putting it in rice”, there’s no shop near here. I’ve checked.

title: Three expedition fuel bottles. All empty.
excerpt: He planned to fill them before it got remote. Unfortunately, it became remote quite gradually.
body:
Anyone on this section of the TET able to bring some petrol? About five litres should do it. Super unleaded preferably.

Bike said 38 miles remaining and the petrol station was only 26 miles away. Apparently that’s in a straight line, which seems a fairly major flaw for a vehicle that uses roads.

Passed a garage earlier but still had two bars, so stopping felt unnecessary. Also spent ages getting past a tractor and didn’t want to throw that away.

Before the preparation police arrive, yes, I carry spare fuel bottles. Three of them. Proper expedition ones.

They’re empty because I didn’t want petrol leaking in the panniers. The plan was to fill them before we got somewhere remote, but it became remote quite gradually.

No, I can’t tell you the road name. There isn’t a road. That was rather the point of the trip.

Happy to reimburse fuel costs. Can do a bank transfer once I’ve moved some money out of savings.

EDIT: Please stop circling the bottles in the photo. I know where they are.

EDIT 2: Someone’s offered to bring regular unleaded. Appreciate the thought, but I’ll hold out another twenty minutes.

title: It ran when I got here. Then I started fixing it.
excerpt: A complete engine rebuild beside a lane. He’s seen people do it to lorries, so nobody’s telling him he can’t.
body:
Anyone near this section got a complete gasket set for an obscure late-80s Italian 350? Not sure which year. Logbook says one thing, engine says another and the owners’ club admin has stopped replying.

Started knocking after breakfast so I’ve stripped it down in the lane. Was only going to check the plug but one thing led to another.

While it’s apart I might as well do a complete rebuild. Does anyone local have crank bearings, piston rings, a torque wrench and somewhere I can plug in a parts washer?

Please don’t start with “you can’t do that at the side of the road”. I’ve seen people in Africa rebuild entire lorry engines beside the road, so nobody’s telling me I can’t sort a single-cylinder bike in Shropshire.

Someone’s already pointed out they were experienced mechanics. Well, they weren’t born experienced, were they.

This is why I bought an older bike. No electronics. Everything’s accessible. Most of it is currently accessible on the blue sheet.

Parts situation isn’t as bad as people make out. Found a piston in Italy. Seller last active in 2017 but I’ve messaged.

Need it back together by four as I’ve only paid for one night at the campsite.

EDIT: The oil wasn’t “neglected”. I’ve topped it up regularly since buying it, so mathematically it’s all been changed.

EDIT 2: Does the arrow on the piston mean the front of the bike or north?

EDIT 3: Please stop suggesting recovery. It ran when I got here. It’s only since I started fixing it that it won’t.

title: Reckon I’ll get another 800 miles out of this?
excerpt: The cords are showing, but the ferry’s booked and there’s plenty of tread on the sides.
body:
Reckon I’ll get another 800 miles out of this?

Setting off tomorrow. Mostly motorway to the ferry, then a few days on the TET. Fully loaded but I’ve left the camping chair at home.

Looks worse in the photo. Only noticed the little threads this morning and they might have been there ages.

Still plenty of tread on the sides. Seems wasteful replacing the entire tyre because of one strip in the middle.

Local place can fit one today but it’s £170. Found the same tyre online for £112, delivery five to seven working days. Can’t really justify being ripped off just because they physically have it.

Please only comment if you’ve actually ridden 800 miles on a tyre exactly like this. Not interested in speculation.

It’s done 9,200 already without any issues, so I’d say it’s proved itself.

EDIT: Yes, the ferry is refundable. That’s not the point. I’ve packed.

EDIT 2: Everyone saying “change it”, I am changing it. I’m asking whether I can do the holiday first.

EDIT 3: Forty-three replies and nobody’s given me the answer I’m looking for. Thought this was an adventure group.

title: Right. It’s on its side. Now what?
excerpt: He followed the group’s advice to the letter. Unfortunately, nobody posted the second step.
body:
Right. It’s on its side. Now what?

Posted earlier about being stuck and several people said “just lie it down”, so I have. It’s been twenty minutes and nothing’s changed.

Is there a second part to this?

Previously I had a bike that wouldn’t go forwards. I now have a bike that won’t go forwards and is lying down. Struggling to see where the improvement is.

Someone’s now saying drag it round. It weighs nearly 300kg. If I could casually drag 300kg through mud I probably wouldn’t have opened Facebook.

Panniers are still attached because nobody mentioned removing them in the original instructions. Please put all the steps in one comment. I’m working through these in chronological order.

Also, whoever said “use the bars”, do you mean the handlebars or crash bars? Be specific. I’ve already pulled quite hard on both.

Can the bloke who suggested this come back online please? Your profile says you’re active.

EDIT: Tried lifting it. Can confirm it’s still the same weight from this angle.

EDIT 2: Sandwiches are in the bottom pannier. This has now affected lunch.

EDIT 3: Please stop liking the photo. This isn’t a trip report.

title: Who do I contact about the width of the TET?
excerpt: The front half fitted. Then both expedition panniers arrived at once.
body:
Who do I contact about the width of the TET?

Found a section that hasn’t been made wide enough for adventure bikes. Front half went through absolutely fine, then both panniers arrived at once.

Wasn’t going fast. Just fast enough that reversing is now a separate problem.

These are proper expedition panniers, so I’m surprised the route hasn’t allowed for them. Surely there’s a standard?

Before everyone starts on packing light, I’m away for four days. I need clothes for riding, clothes for the pub and something respectable in case the pub’s nicer than expected.

The other box is mostly security equipment to stop people stealing the boxes.

Yes, they’re quick-release. The release catches are inside. The lids open outwards. There are currently two substantial pieces of countryside preventing that.

Someone on a little trail bike squeezed past and suggested taking less stuff. Easy to say when your entire luggage system is a sandwich.

Would appreciate practical advice from anyone who’s dealt with this, ideally someone local with two vehicle dollies and no opinions.

EDIT: Tried selecting “narrow roads” on the satnav. No change.

EDIT 2: Please stop suggesting butter. These are powder-coated.

EDIT 3: Cancel the recovery request. A dog walker helped me rock it backwards. Now through with the panniers off. Would still like this marked on the GPX so other expedition riders know there’s some carrying involved.

title: It was going brilliantly until the camping equipment became a trailer.
excerpt: A smaller bike, the same luggage, and a rear subframe that would like a word.
body:
Anyone near the TET with a welder? Rear subframe’s snapped on my CRF250 Rally.

Bought this after everyone said a lighter bike would transform my riding. Transferred all the luggage straight over from the big bike, so it was a very straightforward upgrade.

Was going brilliantly until the camping equipment became a trailer.

Before the usual comments, everything on there is essential. Tent, camp bed, proper pillow, chair, cooking kit, spare cooking kit and a bag of logs because you can’t rely on campsites having decent wood.

Only away for two nights, so there’s hardly any food. Most of the weight is equipment for keeping the food cold.

Haven’t weighed the bags individually, but I can lift each one if someone holds the other handle.

Someone’s mentioned a load limit. I assumed that was for jumps. I’ve been sitting down very carefully over everything.

Ideally need somebody who can weld it without taking the luggage off. Took me three attempts to get the straps right and the loose ends are all neatly tucked away.

Please don’t suggest a hotel. The entire point of camping is saving money.

EDIT: Yes, that’s a full-size camping chair. I tried one of the lightweight ones but you can feel the outdoors through it.

EDIT 2: The straps haven’t moved a millimetre. Happy to recommend those.

EDIT 3: Recovery’s quoted £340. Does anyone know a campsite within pushing distance that offers fabrication?

title: Three screens. No maps. Anyone recognise this junction?
excerpt: He downloaded the route. Didn’t realise the countryside was a separate purchase.
body:
Anyone recognise this junction?

Got a dedicated navigation tablet, backup phone and the bike’s own navigation. Currently three different ways of showing me nothing.

The route is there, but the map underneath has disappeared. I’m a blue triangle in a beige area. Does anyone know which beige area this is?

Apparently I was supposed to download “offline maps”. I downloaded the route. Didn’t realise the countryside was a separate purchase.

Tested everything extensively on the drive last night and it worked perfectly. Wife’s now saying that was because I was connected to the house Wi-Fi, but she doesn’t ride.

Please don’t suggest a paper map. I spent £800 specifically to move beyond paper.

There are two tracks here. One goes uphill and the other also goes uphill but from a different angle. Photo attached. Surely someone local will know.

Managed to get enough signal to post this by walking up a bank. Can someone download the map at their house and send me a screenshot? Ideally all of Wales, but detailed enough to show this gate.

EDIT: Found the coordinates. Didn’t write them down before coming back to where the signal is.

EDIT 2: Backup phone has exactly the same problem. At least that confirms it isn’t the phone.

EDIT 3: A walker’s offered to show me where I am on his map. Will update once he’s finished unfolding it.

title: The Spanish trail has turned into a staircase.
excerpt: He doesn’t speak Spanish, but he took “no, no, no” to mean there were no tolls.
body:
Anyone done this bit of the Spanish TET on a big bike?

Track’s gradually turned into a staircase and I’d like to know when it turns back. Ideally before the bit in the photo.

Spoke to a local at the bottom. Don’t speak Spanish, but he pointed at the bike, shook his head and crossed his arms. Assumed he was saying it was an impressive machine.

He then said “no, no, no”, which I took to mean there were no tolls.

Two lads on little enduro bikes came down wearing knee braces and no luggage. Asked if it was doable and one said “for us, yes”. Found that reassuring at the time.

Bike’s about 320kg with everything on it. Plenty of power, so I’m assuming this is mainly a question of selecting the correct mode.

Please don’t suggest taking the luggage off and walking it up. I walked twenty metres to inspect the first step and had to sit on a rock.

Also, how do you say “could you ride my motorcycle up there while I watch” in Spanish without making it sound like I can’t ride?

Need to be over this hill by six. Booked a lovely hotel on the other side because it looked very close on the map.

EDIT: I know the photo makes it look flat. That’s why I took it from this angle. Wife follows the group.

EDIT 2: Someone’s translated what the local said. Apparently the repeated pointing back towards the village was an important part of the advice.

EDIT 3: Turning round. Can anyone recommend a Spanish phrase for “yes, it’s me again” that doesn’t invite further discussion?

title: It’s October, not January. Why is there snow?
excerpt: He checked the forecast. Rome was 24 degrees. Didn’t think he needed to check every individual bit of Italy.
body:
Anyone else in the Italian Alps finding the weather completely different to what was advertised?

It’s October, not January, and there’s actual snow on the trail. Started as rain, which was disappointing enough, then got ideas above its station.

Packed mesh jacket, summer gloves and waterproof overtrousers. Left the waterproof jacket at home because we were heading south.

Before anyone asks, yes, I checked the forecast. Rome was 24 degrees. Didn’t think I needed to check every individual bit of Italy.

Bike says 2°C, but I’m assuming that’s wind chill because the hotel was much warmer.

Passed three ski lifts on the way up. Thought they were just there for winter.

Does anyone nearby have a spare fleece? Ideally something that packs small, as both panniers are full. One’s mostly clothes for eating outside.

Heated grips are on maximum. Palms are lovely. Unfortunately the rest of me wasn’t included in the winter pack.

Please don’t suggest going down. We spent all morning getting up here and I don’t like wasting progress.

EDIT: The snow in the promotional photos was on the mountains. We’re on the road. I considered those separate things.

EDIT 2: Yes, I know what “Alpine” means. It’s written on my summer gloves.

EDIT 3: Back at the hotel. Bought a fleece in reception for €85. Apparently the little shop I thought was selling souvenirs was selling preparation.

title: Another tyre thread. This one has a spreadsheet.
excerpt: Eleven tyres, a weighted scoring system and 1.8 miles of slightly damp gravel.
body:
Apologies, another tyre thread, but I don’t think anyone’s covered my specific requirements.

I’ve read the previous 146 discussions and unfortunately most contain opinions. Hoping to get something more scientific here, ideally from people who agree with my shortlist.

Planning a fairly demanding mixed-surface expedition next Sunday, weather permitting. Approximately 74 miles of tarmac, 1.8 miles of trail and whatever distance I cover looking for somewhere to turn round.

Bike weighs 247kg before accessories. I’m 94kg without kit, although working on that. Panniers will contain waterproofs, tools, compressor, lunch and my existing tyres’ paperwork.

Riding style: cautious but potentially dynamic.

I need confident motorway manners, complete wet-road security, aggressive mud clearance, minimal noise, excellent mileage and a tread pattern that makes sense when photographed outside a café.

Ideally no compromises.

CURRENT SHORTLIST:

• Continental TKC 80: Visually the correct level of commitment. Concerned about tread-block movement during the faster parts of the journey, particularly the bypass. Can owners describe the movement in millimetres rather than saying “never bothered me”?

• Continental TKC 70: Potentially sensible, which worries me. Would I always wonder what the missing ten could have achieved?

• Michelin Anakee Wild: Strong contender, but how wild? I’m after controlled wildness within a fairly rigid itinerary.

• Michelin Anakee Adventure: This is an adventure, so the naming checks out. Need confirmation that their definition of adventure includes damp agricultural access.

• Pirelli Scorpion Rally STR: Very interested, although I’d like someone to explain which aspects are Scorpion, which are Rally and what proportion of the experience is STR.

• Bridgestone Battlax Adventurecross AX41: Probably the most reassuring number of syllables. Concerned I’ve been influenced by that.

• Dunlop Trailmax Mission: I do have a specific mission, namely reaching the pub without putting a foot down. Would that suit its intended use?

• Dunlop Trailmax Raid: Is Raid above or below Mission? Please don’t answer “different tyres”. I’m trying to establish a hierarchy.

• Heidenau K60 Scout: Several people say they last ages. Useful, but if I choose incorrectly I don’t want to be trapped in a long-term relationship.

• Mitas E-07: My spreadsheet liked this one until someone commented “wooden”, which has required a completely new tab.

• Shinko 804/805: Attractive price, although I’m concerned saving money might undermine the amount of research I’ve done.

I’m also considering mixing brands front and rear, provided both manufacturers are comfortable with each other.

My main concern is the transition from dry gravel into damp gravel and then, potentially, actual mud. I don’t want a tyre that performs brilliantly in the first two phases only to abandon me during the third.

Has anyone measured the point at which damp becomes wet? Preferably in British soil. Reports from Portugal aren’t much use unless you’ve corrected for sunshine.

I’ve prepared a weighted scoring system:

Wet tarmac: 22%
Dry tarmac: 18%
Gravel: 17%
Mud evacuation: 16%
Longevity: 14%
Noise: 8%
How they look with aluminium luggage: 5%

My wife suggested adding “actually going for a ride”, but there isn’t room without compromising the model.

Pressure recommendations welcome, but please state ambient temperature, altitude, breakfast weight and whether your gauge has been independently verified. “I run mine at 30” tells me nothing about your relationship with accuracy.

Also, when people describe a tyre as 50/50, is that by mileage or time? Because I expect the 1.8 miles of trail to take approximately as long as the motorway section.

Please include your bike, tyre sizes, mileage, load, riding experience and whether your confidence comes from training or simply having survived previous decisions.

No “just ride what you’ve got” comments. What I’ve got is almost new, which makes this decision especially difficult to explain at home.

EDIT: I’ve postponed Sunday. Two recommendations have come in since I thought we’d reached a consensus.

EDIT 2: A local says he regularly does the route on a delivery scooter. Does anyone know what tyres those come with?

The photo shows the level of extreme conditions I’ll be riding in. You can’t really appreciate the moisture gradient from the picture.

title: Day six in the wilderness. Dad’s garage is in the background.
excerpt: A quick base-layer question. Absolutely not promoting anything. Follow first so she knows you’re interested.
body:
Hey adventure family 🏍️✨ Quick base-layer question! Hope this is allowed, absolutely NOT promoting anything.

Day six completely solo in the wilderness and these thermals have honestly been a game changer. Eight hours of deep mud today, three river crossings and not another human for miles. Just me, the bike and the elements 🤍

Anyway, merino or synthetic? Would love your advice before I film my definitive guide to choosing the right one.

Please leave detailed answers on my latest reel rather than here as it helps me keep all the knowledge in one place. Follow first so I know you’re genuinely interested in riding.

A few people asked how these perform under armour. Haven’t tried that combination yet because it hides the waistband, but I’ve tested them extensively standing beside the bike.

They’ve kept me comfortable from the frozen mountain passes this morning to the desert section just after lunch. Not sure of the temperatures. My weather app keeps insisting I’m in Surrey.

For everyone asking about the fit, there’s a full 19-minute walkaround on my channel, plus a separate video of the back. The fabric information is coming in part three once the brand replies.

Again, just here for advice. But if you want the exact set I’ve already decided is the best, use code REMOTE15.

Please don’t turn this into a technical thread. Someone’s asked about moisture retention and I’d like to keep things welcoming.

EDIT: That isn’t a garage. It’s our remote expedition accommodation.

EDIT 2: The wheelie bin belongs to the accommodation. Even remote communities deserve waste collection.

EDIT 3: The ring light is emergency equipment. Being visible is incredibly important.

EDIT 4: Yes, I said solo. My photographer doesn’t ride, so he doesn’t count.

EDIT 5: The boots are spotless because I look after my kit. No, I haven’t removed the packaging from inside them. It helps maintain the shape between adventures.

EDIT 6: Whoever’s posted the Street View of my dad’s house, please respect expedition security.

Anyway, merino or synthetic? Comments on the reel please. This post isn’t converting.

title: Six weeks of practice. Someone else’s 1290.
excerpt: Her teal kit matches the little bike. His orange kit matches the big one. Please stop asking about that.
body:
Six weeks ago I was nervous doing a U-turn and now I’m riding my 1290 through stuff like this 😍

Had a couple of practice sessions in a car park and something just clicked. Honestly think people overcomplicate big bikes. Once you stop worrying about the weight you barely notice it.

My boyfriend has been riding for years and even he couldn’t believe what he was seeing.

Would anyone be interested in some videos about building confidence on a bigger bike? I’ve already put a few on my Instagram, link in bio. Give me a follow and comment CONFIDENCE on the latest reel and I’ll send you the others.

Not an instructor or anything, just think it helps seeing someone normal doing it rather than the same old blokes telling everyone they need more training.

This section was properly technical. Doesn’t look much in the photos but some of those steps were huge. Had to stop a few times to get my breath back and check the pictures.

Quite pleased with how relaxed I look on the bike now. Used to be so tense even sitting on one.

For those asking about my kit, I’ve tagged everything on Instagram. The teal looks AMAZING in the mountains. Discount code should be working by tonight so hold off ordering until then please.

We didn’t get any riding footage unfortunately. My boyfriend said he was too busy, which is annoying because he had plenty of time to stand in the background of all my photos.

Might go back and film it another day. Depends whether he’ll bring the bike again.

EDIT: Bring it in the van. Obviously I ride it.

The little bike is also ours. Not sure why everyone’s so interested in that when this post is about the 1290.

Yes, my helmet matches it. I bought the helmet because I liked the colour. His kit is orange because he likes orange. You lot need a hobby.

Someone’s asked why the keys are clipped to his jacket. Because my trousers haven’t got pockets.

Anyway if you want to follow the rest of the trip it’ll all be on my stories. Please put questions there as I don’t always check this group unless I’ve posted something.

EDIT: He’s asked me to clarify that I haven’t ridden the rocky bit yet. I meant this sort of terrain generally. We’ve ridden past loads of it.

Comments turned off. Was only trying to inspire people.

title: £280 of tools. None of them fit the nut.
excerpt: The titanium toolkit is immaculate. The rear wheel remains firmly attached.
body:
Anyone near this lane with a bigger spanner?

Before this turns into another lecture about preparation, please look at the photo. I have brought considerably more tools than most people own.

Rear puncture. Got a spare tube, patches, tyre levers, compressor, valve tool, spare valve cores, nitrile gloves and a little mat so the parts don’t get dirty.

Unfortunately none of the spanners fit the nut holding the wheel on.

Biggest one stops just short of going over it. Have tried approaching from both sides.

Spent £280 putting this kit together after watching a bloke unpack his on YouTube. Followed his list exactly. Apparently he has a different bike, which wasn’t mentioned until quite a long way into the video.

Everything is titanium where possible. Saved nearly 400 grams compared with ordinary tools, although I’ve brought the ordinary ones as well in case the titanium is too nice to use.

Please don’t ask whether I tested it at home. There wasn’t anything wrong with the bike at home.

The little ratchet is lovely. Can get the screen off, both mirrors off and access the air filter. None of those are currently the problem, but I’ve checked.

Someone’s suggested an adjustable spanner. Deliberately didn’t bring one because a bloke in the comments said they’re for people who don’t know what they’re doing. Starting to think I’m exactly who they’re for.

Also, once the nut is off, how are we supporting the bike? The video cut from him pointing at the wheel to it being on a bench.

I’ve got cable ties if that helps. Everyone says you can fix anything with cable ties but nobody ever gets into the details.

Would really appreciate someone coming out. You only need to bring the spanner. You’re welcome to use all my other equipment, provided it goes back in the correct pockets.

EDIT: The compressor works brilliantly. We’ve confirmed the puncture six times now.

EDIT 2: Found the original toolkit under the seat. There’s a big flat spanner in it.

EDIT 3: Yes, it fits.

EDIT 4: Going to leave this up because other people might learn something. Please stop tagging me in it. It’s my post.

title: Five miles of contingency. Four hours of solar charging.
excerpt: The phone is on 100%. The Zero is still on zero. He’d appreciate nobody mentioning the diesel recovery van.
body:
Anyone near this section of the TET with electricity?

First proper outing on the Zero. Worked the route out very carefully last night. Dash said 80 miles, route was 75. That’s five whole miles of contingency, so please don’t start with poor planning.

Bike stopped at 68.

Yes, there were hills. They were on the map when I calculated it, so I assumed they’d been included.

Did a couple of extra runs up one section because my mate missed the video, but they were only short. Also came back down, which I understood put it back in.

Anyway, I’m not completely unprepared. Brought a folding solar panel for exactly this situation. Plugged it into the USB socket and have been sitting here for nearly four hours.

Absolutely no difference.

Panel says it’s suitable for outdoor adventures. There’s a picture of a mountain on the box. Not sure how much more specific I was supposed to be.

It is overcast, but it’s clearly daytime. I can see the panel.

Have moved it three times to follow the brightest bit of cloud. Also wiped it with the expensive visor cloth rather than the ordinary one.

Someone’s saying the USB socket is an output. Surely that depends which end you’re standing at?

Please explain in normal terms. A bloke’s just sent me a calculation involving kilowatt-hours and according to him I need to stay until Thursday. He hasn’t said which Thursday.

I don’t need a full charge. Just enough to get to the charger I drove past earlier because it was £1.20 more expensive.

Starting to get hungry. Already eaten the emergency flapjack and the flapjack I was keeping in case the emergency got worse.

EDIT: Panel charges my phone fine. Now on 100%. Bike still on zero. At least I can keep updating everyone.

EDIT 2: Have unplugged it from the bike following several increasingly firm explanations.

EDIT 3: Mate’s coming with his diesel van. Would appreciate it if nobody mentions this under my post about energy independence.

title: No finance. No servicing. No forward movement.
excerpt: An £850 trail bike, the original chain, and an owner who calls every warning sign character.
body:
Just a reminder you don’t need a £20,000 adventure bike to get out there 👍

Bought this old girl for £850. No finance, no riding modes, no expensive servicing. Just proper old-fashioned engineering.

Currently waiting for my brother with a trailer, but that’s unrelated.

Chain’s come off again. Put it back on at breakfast and it stayed on for nearly an hour, so something must have changed.

Before everyone starts, I do maintain it. Sprayed the chain this morning. You can see the can in the photo.

Apparently the sprocket teeth are supposed to be a different shape. I assumed they leaned forward to help pull the chain round. Looked quite clever actually.

Previous owner said it had never let him down. Starting to wonder how far from his house he went.

There was a rattling noise when I bought it but the bloke said “they all do that” and I respected his experience. He’d owned it for eleven days.

Had a garage look at it last month. They suggested a chain, both sprockets, wheel bearings and fork seals. Came to nearly what I paid for the bike, so obviously I went somewhere else.

Second place said much the same. Small town though. They probably know each other.

People keep saying preventative maintenance. I prefer to deal with actual problems rather than paying for things that haven’t happened. Admittedly several have now happened together, which is inconvenient.

The fork oil leak has nearly stopped on its own, so that’s one thing off the list.

Please don’t criticise the seat. That tape’s been on there longer than most of you have been riding.

Anyway, still been a cracking day. Lovely scenery, met some walkers, had plenty of time to appreciate both.

If anyone’s passing, could you bring a sandwich? Mine’s at the next campsite with everything else I confidently sent ahead.

EDIT: Brother’s asked whether this is the same chain he told me to replace at Christmas. Not sure why the date matters.

EDIT 2: Someone’s called it a rolling restoration. Bit generous at the moment.

EDIT 3: Home now. Brother reckons I should sell it. Absolutely not. Spent the whole journey explaining how much money it’s saved me.

title: All that power. Still can’t leave the parking space.
alts: A loaded KTM parked nose-down toward a closed farm gate
excerpt: A KTM 1290 owner discovers a situation where all the power is pointing the wrong way.
body:
Anyone nearby able to help move a KTM 1290 about six feet?

Nothing wrong with it. Absolutely phenomenal machine. Just parked facing slightly downhill for a photo and now need to go in the direction it doesn’t do.

Gate’s locked. Too narrow to turn round. Tried paddling backwards but I’m mainly moving gravel into my boots.

Please don’t suggest a smaller bike. Test rode a middleweight and felt it lacked the overtaking power I need. Currently being overtaken by a woman walking a spaniel.

Bought the 1290 because I didn’t want to find myself in a situation where I needed more power. Turns out I’ve found a situation where none of it is pointing the right way.

Have tried getting off and pulling it. Moved it about an inch, needed a rest, then lost the inch getting back on.

Panniers are full because this is an adventure. If I wanted to travel without luggage I’d have bought a bicycle.

Also filled the tank right before coming down here. Was quite pleased with myself for planning ahead.

Someone’s suggested taking everything off to make it lighter. That’s my afternoon unpacked across a farm entrance, then. Is there anything in the settings I could try first?

Dealer spent twenty minutes explaining the electronics. At no point did he demonstrate leaving a parking space.

Before anyone asks, yes, I saw the slope when I parked. I assumed it would feel less steep once I’d finished my sandwich.

The photo wasn’t even very good. Can’t see the exhaust, which was most of the reason for stopping.

If two reasonably strong people could come out I reckon we’d have it done in seconds. Please don’t bring cameras. Already enough photos of this location.

EDIT: It is in neutral. Thank you to the fourteen people who thought I’d spent an hour trying to pull it backwards in gear.

EDIT 2: Spaniel woman’s husband has arrived. He’s asked why I didn’t park the other way round. Would really appreciate some fresh ideas.

EDIT 3: Out now. Three of us pushed it back. Lovely couple. Unfortunately he’s on this group.

EDIT 4: Still wouldn’t swap it for anything smaller. You need to ride one to understand.

title: Somewhere safe. Preferably with your bike in it.
excerpt: An unusually specific request for overnight parking, undone by a very reflective shop window.
body:
Alright lads. Coming up from south London to do some Oxfordshire countryside riding this weekend. Anyone got somewhere safe I could leave my bike overnight?

Preferably in a garage with your own bike. Just feel more comfortable knowing another decent bike’s in there. Shows you take security seriously.

What do you ride out of interest?

Someone’s offered a locked shed but only keeps gardening stuff in it. Appreciate it mate, not really what I’m looking for.

Ideally another adventure rider with something fairly new. Nothing against older bikes, just trying to meet people with similar interests and resale values.

Sorry, riding values. Autocorrect.

Pic of mine attached. Lovely thing. Only recently got into these so don’t ask me loads of technical questions about what model it is.

Can’t stay and chat unfortunately. Very busy itinerary. Might have a mate collect me in his van so I don’t disturb anyone starting the bike early.

No need to move your bike out to make room. Honestly. Leave it exactly where it is.

Why’s everyone recommending hotels? Trying to get involved in the community here.

Also whoever’s offered to come riding with me, cheers but I prefer the parking side of adventure riding at the moment.

EDIT: Balaclava’s for the cold.

EDIT 2: Gloves are also for the cold. Yes, I know the bloke reflected across the road is in a T-shirt. People feel temperatures differently.

EDIT 3: That’s not me in the window.

EDIT 4: Obviously it’s me taking the photo. I meant that’s not what I usually wear.

EDIT 5: Bike belongs to a mate. Said “mine” to keep the post simple.

EDIT 6: Don’t know why he’s commented saying we’ve never met. Only spoke briefly outside the shop.

Never mind. Sorted now. Can an admin delete this including the pictures people have saved please.

title: Who do I complain to about the gates?
alts: An ordinary farm gate, grazing livestock and a few droppings on a gravel track
excerpt: Nine gates, several cowpats and a city rider who thought the countryside would be finished by now.
body:
Who do I complain to about the gates?

First day on the TET after riding down from London and I’ve opened nine already. Nine. Then had to close them all again because apparently that’s also my responsibility.

I came here to ride a motorcycle. So far I’ve mainly been operating agricultural doors.

Most aren’t even locked. They’re just closed for the sake of it.

Asked a farmer why there were so many and he said “cattle”. Not particularly helpful. I could already see those.

Surely the cows know which field they live in? They’ve been here longer than I have.

And the mess. Cow poo, horse poo, absolutely everywhere. Some of it looks recent, so whatever cleaning arrangement they’ve got clearly isn’t working.

You’d be fined for that where I live. Watched a horse do it while its owner just carried on talking to her friend. Didn’t even reach for a bag.

When I mentioned it she said it’s good for the roses. There aren’t any roses on this track. There is, however, my front tyre.

Got some on my boots opening gate number seven. These boots were £380. I don’t think it’s unreasonable to expect the handle area to be kept clean.

Also a tractor came past and I had to pull over into the hedge. No apology. Driver gave me a little wave as though we’d both enjoyed it.

Is there a quieter time to visit when the farming isn’t happening? The website photos made it look finished.

Before anyone says I should have expected mud, I did. Bought the off-road mudguard specifically. Nobody mentioned it would contain ingredients.

There’s a smell near the big shed as well. Difficult to describe but it’s very farm-like. Would be fine occasionally, but we stopped for lunch and it continued throughout.

I love the countryside. That’s why I came. Just think a few basic improvements would make it much more accessible to people who don’t already work in it.

EDIT: Yes, I shut every gate. I’ve got photos of all nine if that’s what this group needs.

EDIT 2: Someone’s suggested a cattle grid. Happy to download it if it means fewer gates. Is it better than the GPX?

EDIT 3: Back at the hotel. They’ve asked me to leave my boots outside. Finally, someone taking this seriously.

title: Five miles. Forty-six takes. One epic adventure.
alts: A fictional rider jumping a small bump on a blue rally bike
The same rider rounding a gravel corner in a cloud of dust
The rider posing beside her bike at sunset
excerpt: Dust, jumps and a stunning sunset. The hotel is still visible, but that’s not what it’s about.
body:
What an absolutely unreal day on the trails 😍 Dust, jumps, mountain views and finishing with THAT sunset. Honestly having the most amazing adventure.

A few favourites from today. Full film on YouTube Sunday, assuming we can get forty minutes out of it.

Before someone posts the tracking screenshot again, yes, we covered five miles. I don’t know why this needs to be an issue. That’s not what it’s about.

We left at nine and didn’t finish until sunset. I was exhausted. You don’t need to ride hundreds of miles to have a proper day on the bike.

The jump took most of the morning. First few goes were fine but you couldn’t really see daylight under the tyres. Then we got the angle right but my ponytail was tucked in.

Had to go back for the thumbnail because I looked too comfortable and the video’s called “I DIDN’T THINK I’D MAKE IT”.

Really pleased with the corner shot. Did it eleven times before the dust went in the right direction. Then waited for it to settle so we could film me arriving somewhere nobody had been.

My boyfriend said we could probably get moving at that point, but the light was getting harsh so we stopped for lunch.

Spent the afternoon recording a little chat about escaping schedules and just seeing where the trail takes you. Had to restart because he walked through the background carrying the tripods.

Then it was nearly golden hour and obviously you don’t ride away from a location when it’s about to look that good.

The sunset photo is probably my favourite. Such a peaceful moment. Just me, the bike and him saying “are we done?” from behind the camera.

Some people seem genuinely annoyed that I’m enjoying myself without putting big numbers on the dash. Not everything has to be a competition.

For clarity, the five miles includes going back for the cameras. The hotel is still visible from the jump, but only if you look behind you, which isn’t really my outlook.

We’re staying there again tonight. They hadn’t finished cleaning our room when we asked for it back.

Anyway, which photo should be the thumbnail? Please comment on Instagram rather than here because I’ve already put the poll up.

Kit links are in my bio. Dust is my own.

EDIT: Someone’s worked out you can see the same bush in all three shots. Yes. We formed quite a connection with the area.

EDIT 2: No, the route guide doesn’t need updating. We just haven’t reached the first instruction yet.

EDIT 3: Tomorrow’s supposed to be a bigger day. Found a puddle about half a mile further on that could easily be a two-part episode.
